items.sentence_raw: From a number of recent studies, it has become clear that blind people can appreciate the use of outlines and perspectives to describe the arrangement of objects and other surfaces in space.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says blind people can *'appreciate the use of outlines and perspectives'* — **'perspectives'** is a convention in art. So they can **recognise conventions such as perspective**. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: But pictures are more than literal representations.
This fact was drawn to my attention dramatically when a blind woman in one of my investigations decided on her own initiative to draw a wheel as it was spinning.
items.explain: Q28: The writer was surprised because the blind woman drew a curve inside the circle *'to show this motion'* — she included a symbol for movement. The passage says *'lines of motion... are a very recent invention'*, so this was unexpected. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: To show this motion, she traced a curve inside the circle (Fig. 1).
items.explain: Q28: The writer was surprised because the blind woman drew a curve inside the circle *'to show this motion'* — she included a symbol for movement. The passage says *'lines of motion... are a very recent invention'*, so this was unexpected. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: I was taken aback.
Lines of motion, such as the one she used, are a very recent invention in the history of illustration.
Indeed, as art scholar David Kunzle notes, Wilhelm Busch, a trend-setting nineteenth-century cartoonist, used virtually no motion lines in his popular figures until about 1877.
When I asked several other blind study subjects to draw a spinning wheel, one particularly clever rendition appeared repeatedly: several subjects showed the wheel's spokes as curved lines.
When asked about these curves, they all described them as metaphorical ways of suggesting motion.
Majority rule would argue that this device somehow indicated motion very well.
But was it a better indicator than, say, broken or wavy lines - or any other kind of line, for that matter?
The answer was not clear.
So I decided to test whether various lines of motion were apt ways of showing movement or if they were merely idiosyncratic marks.
Moreover, I wanted to discover whether there were differences in how the blind and the sighted interpreted lines of motion.
To search out these answers, I created raised-line drawings of five different wheels, depicting spokes with lines that curved, bent, waved, dashed and extended beyond the perimeter of the wheel.
I then asked eighteen blind volunteers to feel the wheels and assign one of the following motions to each wheel: wobbling, spinning fast, spinning steadily, jerking or braking.
My control group consisted of eighteen sighted undergraduates from the University of Toronto.
All but one of the blind subjects assigned distinctive motions to each wheel.

Most guessed that the curved spokes indicated that the wheel was spinning steadily; the wavy spokes, they thought, suggested that the wheel was wobbling; and the bent spokes were taken as a sign that the wheel was jerking.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says *'curved spokes indicated that the wheel was spinning steadily'* — **'spinning steadily'** means **steady spinning**. Diagram A shows curved spokes. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Subjects assumed that spokes extending beyond the wheel's perimeter signified that the wheel had its brakes on and that dashed spokes indicated the wheel was spinning quickly.
items.explain:
Q30: The passage says *'spokes extending beyond the wheel's perimeter signified that the wheel had its brakes on'*. Diagram E shows spokes going past the wheel's edge. So the answer is **E**.

Q31: The passage says *'dashed spokes indicated the wheel was spinning quickly'* — **'spinning quickly'** means **rapid spinning**. Diagram C shows dashed spokes. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: In addition, the favored description for the sighted was the favored description for the blind in every instance.
What is more, the consensus among the sighted was barely higher than that among the blind.
Because motion devices are unfamiliar to the blind, the task I gave them involved some problem solving.
Evidently, however, the blind not only figured out meanings for each line of motion, but as a group they generally came up with the same meaning at least as frequently as did sighted subjects.
items.explain: Q29: The passage says the blind *'figured out meanings for each line of motion'* and *'came up with the same meaning'* as sighted people. This means they had a **good understanding of symbols representing movement**. The answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: We have found that the blind understand other kinds of visual metaphors as well.
One blind woman drew a picture of a child inside a heart - choosing that symbol, she said, to show that love surrounded the child.
With Chang Hong Liu, a doctoral student from China, I have begun exploring how well blind people understand the symbolism behind shapes such as hearts that do not directly represent their meaning.
We gave a list of twenty pairs of words to sighted subjects and asked them to pick from each pair the term that best related to a circle and the term that best related to a square.
items.explain:
Q33: The passage says they gave *'a list of twenty pairs of words'* to subjects. So the blank needs **'pairs'** — the answer is **G**.

Q34: The experiment investigated how people perceived symbolism in abstract **'shapes'** like circles and squares. The passage says they asked which term related to a circle or a square. So the answer is **H**.

items.sentence_raw: For example, we asked: What goes with soft?
A circle or a square?
Which shape goes with hard?
All our subjects deemed the circle soft and the square hard.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says *'All our subjects deemed the circle soft and the square hard'* — these subjects were **sighted** volunteers. So the answer is **I**.

items.sentence_raw: A full 94% ascribed happy to the circle, instead of sad.
But other pairs revealed less agreement: 79% matched fast to slow and weak to strong, respectively.
And only 51% linked deep to circle and shallow to square.
items.explain:
Q36: The passage says *'only 51% linked deep to circle and shallow to square'* — these were the **sighted** volunteers. So the answer is **I**.

Q37: The 51% figure refers to the word pair **'deep'** and shallow. The blank asks what was assigned to a circle, so the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: (See Fig. 2)
When we tested four totally blind volunteers using the same list, we found that their choices closely resembled those made by the sighted subjects.
items.explain:
Q38: The test was later repeated with *'four totally blind volunteers'* — so the blank needs **'blind'**. The answer is **B**.

Q39: The passage says the blind volunteers' choices *'closely resembled'* those of the sighted — **'closely resembled'** means **similar**. So the answer is **J**.

items.sentence_raw: One man, who had been blind since birth, scored extremely well.
He made only one match differing from the consensus, assigning 'far' to square and 'near' to circle.
In fact, only a small majority of sighted subjects - 53% - had paired far and near to the opposite partners.
Thus, we concluded that the blind interpret abstract shapes as sighted people do.
items.explain: Q40: The writer's conclusion is that *'the blind interpret abstract shapes as sighted people do'* — this means they **comprehend visual metaphors in similar ways**. The answer is **B**.
